- _Fagus tortuosa_ (Dippel) F.Boden | _**Fagus sylvatica**_, the **European beech** or **common beech**, is a large [deciduous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deciduous "Deciduous") tree in the [beech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagaceae "Fagaceae") family with smooth silvery-grey bark, large leaf area, and a short trunk with low branches.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-3) It is native to much of Europe, growing in humid climates. The species is cultivated as an [ornamental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ornamental_plant "Ornamental plant"), and has been spread beyond its original range, including in North America. Numerous cultivars have been developed, including the showy copper beech, _Fagus sylvatica purpurea_. Although slightly toxic due to the [tannins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tannin "Tannin") and [alkaloids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alkaloid "Alkaloid") they contain, the [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit) "Nut (fruit)") are consumed by animals and humans. The trees are used for timber, such as the making of furniture. ## Description _Fagus sylvatica_ is a large [tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree "Tree"), capable of reaching heights of up to 50 metres (160 feet) tall[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-4) and 3m (10ft) trunk diameter, though more typically 25–35m (82–115ft) tall and up to 1.5m (5ft) trunk diameter. A 10-year-old sapling will stand about 4m (13ft) tall. Undisturbed, the European beech has a lifespan of 300 years; one tree at the Valle Cervara site was more than 500 years old, the oldest known in the northern hemisphere.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-5) In cultivated forest stands trees are normally harvested at 80–120 years of age.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-6) 30 years are needed to attain full maturity (as compared to 40 for [American beech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_grandifolia "Fagus grandifolia")). Like most trees, its form depends on the location; in forest areas, _F.sylvatica_ grows to over 30m (98ft), with branches being high up on the trunk. In open locations, it will become much shorter (typically 20m (66ft)) but more massive with a broader crown and stouter trunk. The [leaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leaves "Leaves") are alternate, simple, and entire or with a slightly [crenate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crenate "Crenate") margin, 5–10cm (2–3+7⁄8in) long and 3–7cm (1.2–2.8in) broad, with 6–7 veins on each side of the leaf (as opposed to 7–10 veins in _[F.orientalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_orientalis "Fagus orientalis")_). When crenate, there is one point at each vein tip, never any points between the veins. The [buds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud "Bud") are long and slender, 15–30mm (5⁄8–1+1⁄8in) long and 2–3mm (3⁄32–1⁄8in) thick, but thicker, up to 4–5mm (1⁄8–1⁄4in), where the buds include flower buds. The leaves of beech are often not [abscissed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abscission "Abscission") (dropped) in the autumn and instead remain on the tree until the spring. This process is called [marcescence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcescence "Marcescence"). This particularly occurs when trees are [saplings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapling "Sapling") or when plants are clipped as a hedge (making beech hedges attractive screens, even in winter), but it also often continues to occur on the lower branches when the tree is mature. The species is [monoecious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monoecious "Monoecious"). The male flowers are borne in small [catkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catkin "Catkin"),[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-7) a hallmark of the [Fagales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagales "Fagales") order. The female flowers produce beechnuts, small triangular [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit) "Nut (fruit)") 15–20mm (5⁄8–3⁄4in) long and 7–10mm (1⁄4–3⁄8in) wide at the base; there are two nuts in each cupule, maturing in the autumn 5–6 months after pollination. Flower and seed production is particularly abundant in years following a hot, sunny and dry summer, though rarely for two years in a row. Small quantities of seeds may be produced around 10 years of age, but not a heavy crop until the tree is at least 30 years old. Spring leaf budding by the European beech is triggered by a combination of day length and temperature. Bud break each year is from the middle of April to the beginning of May, often with remarkable precision (within a few days). It is more precise in the north of its range than the south, and at 600m (2,000ft) than at [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_level "Sea level").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-8) - replaces it further east. In the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"), it shows some [hybridisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hybrid_(biology) "Hybrid (biology)") with oriental beech; these hybrid trees are named _[Fagus × taurica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_%C3%97_taurica "Fagus × taurica")_ Popl. \[ _Fagus moesiaca_ (Domin, Maly) Czecz.\]. In the southern part of its range around the [Mediterranean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") and [Sicily](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sicily "Sicily"),[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-14) it grows only in mountain forests, at 600–1,800m (1,969–5,906ft) altitude. Although often regarded as native in southern England, recent evidence suggests that _F. sylvatica_ did not arrive in England until about 4000 [BCE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BCE "BCE"), or 2,000 years subsequent to the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel") forming following the [ice ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period "Last Glacial Period"); it could have been an early introduction by [Stone Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_Age "Stone Age") humans, who used the [nuts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nut_(fruit) "Nut (fruit)") for food.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-15) The beech is classified as a native in the south of England and as a non-native in the north where it is often removed from 'native' woods.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-16) Localised pollen records have been recorded in the North of England from the [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age") by Sir [Harry Godwin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Godwin "Harry Godwin"). Changing climatic conditions may put beech populations in southern England under increased stress and while it may not be possible to maintain the current levels of beech in some sites it is thought that conditions for beech in north-west England will remain favourable or even improve. It is often planted in Britain. Similarly, the nature of Norwegian beech populations is subject to debate. If native, they would represent the northern range of the species, although molecular genetic analyses imply that these populations represent intentional introduction from Denmark before and during the [Viking Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age "Viking Age").[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-17) The beech in [Vestfold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestfold "Vestfold") and at Seim north of [Bergen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen "Bergen") in Norway is now spreading naturally and regarded as [native](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Native_plant "Native plant").[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-18) The European beech tolerates a variety of soil types, but requires a humid atmosphere (with precipitation well distributed throughout the year) and well-drained soil. It prefers moderately fertile ground, calcified or lightly acidic, so it is found more often on the side of a hill than at the bottom of clayey basin. It tolerates rigorous winter cold, but is sensitive to spring frost. In Norway's oceanic climate planted trees grow well north to [Bodø Municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bod%C3%B8_Municipality "Bodø Municipality"), and produce seedlings and can spread naturally in Trondheim.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-19) In Sweden, beech trees do not grow as far north as in Norway.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-20) In the woodlands of southern Britain, beech is dominant over oak and elm south of a line from about north Suffolk across to Cardigan. Oak are the dominant forest trees north of this line. One of the most beautiful European beech forests called [Sonian Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonian_Forest "Sonian Forest") ( _Forêt de Soignes/Zoniënwoud_) is found in the southeast of Brussels, Belgium. Beech is a dominant tree species in France and constitutes about 10% of French forests. The largest [virgin forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virgin_forest "Virgin forest") made of beech trees are [Uholka-Shyrokyi Luh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uholka-Shyrokyi_Luh_primeval_beech_forest "Uholka-Shyrokyi Luh primeval beech forest") (8,800 hectares or 22,000 acres) in Ukraine[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Commarmot-2013-21) and Izvoarele Nerei (5,012ha or 12,380 acres in one forest body) in [Semenic-Cheile Carașului National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semenic-Cheile_Cara%C8%99ului_National_Park "Semenic-Cheile Carașului National Park"), [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania"). These habitats are the home of Europe's largest predators, the brown bear, the grey wolf, and the lynx.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-24) Many trees are older than 350 years in Izvoarele Nerei[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-25) and even 500 years in Uholka-Shyrokyi Luh.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Commarmot-2013-21) ## Ecology ### Symbioses The root system is shallow, even superficial, with large roots spreading out in all directions. European beech forms [ectomycorrhizas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ectomycorrhiza "Ectomycorrhiza") with a range of fungi including many _[Russula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russula "Russula")_ species, as well as _[Laccaria amethystina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laccaria_amethystina "Laccaria amethystina")_,[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Packham-2012-26) and with the species _[Ramaria flavosaponaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramaria_flavosaponaria "Ramaria flavosaponaria")_.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Agerer-2012-27) _[Tomentella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tomentella "Tomentella")_ Pat. species and _[Cenococcum geophilum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenococcum_geophilum "Cenococcum geophilum")_ have been found in Danish and Spanish beech forests. These fungi are important in enhancing uptake of water and nutrients from the soil.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-Packham-2012-26) ### Diseases [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Detail_of_Biscogniauxia_nummularia.JPG/500px-Detail_of_Biscogniauxia_nummularia.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Detail_of_Biscogniauxia_nummularia.JPG) [Beech tarcrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscogniauxia_nummularia "Biscogniauxia nummularia") causes strip-canker and wood rot. _Fagus sylvatica_ and other beeches are prone to false heartwood ('red heart') a condition where drought, nutrient deficient soil, branch breakage, pathogen infestation or other stressor induces formation of protection wood.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-28) False heartwood often manifests in the areas of the trunk associated with [symplastless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Symplast "Symplast") branches. As branch symplast dies, the trunk wood becomes depleted of nitrogen-containing molecules essential for life; this increases risk of catastrophic trunk failure.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-29) As the European beech exhibits deterministic leaf and shoot development and has a larger leaf area than other European hardwood trees, it is relatively more sensitive to drought and may respond to a dry summer with pre-senescent [leafdrop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abscission "Abscission").[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-30) _[Biscogniauxia nummularia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biscogniauxia_nummularia "Biscogniauxia nummularia")_ (beech tarcrust) is an [ascomycete](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ascomycota "Ascomycota") primary pathogen of beech trees, causing strip-canker and wood rot. It can be found at all times of year and is not edible.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-31) ## Cultivation European beech is a popular ornamental tree in parks and large gardens in [temperate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperateness "Temperateness") regions of the world. In North America, it is preferred for this purpose over the native _[Fagus grandifolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_grandifolia "Fagus grandifolia")_, which despite its tolerance of warmer climates, is slower growing, taking an average of 10 years longer to attain maturity. The town of [Brookline, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brookline,_Massachusetts "Brookline, Massachusetts") has one of the largest, if not the largest, grove of European beech trees in the United States. The 2.5-acre (1ha) public park, called 'The Longwood Mall', was planted sometime before 1850, qualifying it as the oldest stand of European beeches in the U.S.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-32) Since the early 19th century numerous [cultivars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultivar "Cultivar") of European beech have been made by horticultural selection, often repeatedly; they include: - copper beech or purple beech ( _Fagus sylvatica purpurea_)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-33) – a mutation of the European beech which was first noted in 1690 in the "Possenwald" forest near the town of [Sondershausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sondershausen "Sondershausen") in Thuringia, Germany. It is assumed that about 99% of all copper beeches in the world are descendants of this copper beech. Its leaves are purple, often turning deep spinach green by mid-summer. In the United States Charles Sprague Sargent noted the earliest appearance in a nurseryman's catalogue in 1820, but in 1859 "the finest copper beech in America... more than fifty feet high" was noted in the grounds of Thomas Ash, Esq., [Throggs Neck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Throggs_Neck "Throggs Neck"), New York;[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-34) it must have been more than forty years old at the time. - They were also ground to make flour, which could be eaten after the tannins were leached out by soaking.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-44)[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-46) Additionally, _Primary Product AM 01_, a smoke flavouring, is produced from _F.sylvatica._[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-47) ### Timber The timber of the European beech is used in the manufacture of numerous objects and implements. Its fine and short grain makes it an easy wood to work with, easy to soak, dye, varnish and glue. Steaming makes the wood even easier to machine. It has an excellent finish and is resistant to compression and splitting, and it is stiff when flexed. Milling is sometimes difficult due to cracking. The density of the wood is 720 kilograms (1,590 pounds) per cubic metre.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-48) It is particularly well suited for minor carpentry, particularly furniture. From chairs to [parquetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parquetry "Parquetry") (flooring) and staircases, the European beech can do almost anything other than heavy structural support, so long as it is not left outdoors. Its hardness make it ideal for making wooden [mallets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mallet "Mallet") and [workbench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workbench "Workbench") tops. The wood rots easily if it is not protected by a tar based on a distillate of its own bark (as used in [railway sleepers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad_tie "Railroad tie")).[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-49)[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-50) It is better for [paper pulp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulp_(paper) "Pulp (paper)") than many other broadleaved trees though is only sometimes used for this, the high cellulose content can also be spun into [modal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modal_(textile) "Modal (textile)"), which is used as a textile akin to cotton. The code for its use in Europe is fasy (from _FA_ gus _SY_ lvatica). Common beech is also considered one of the best [firewoods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firewood "Firewood") for fireplaces.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-51) - [![Old stand of beech prepared for regeneration (note the young undergrowth) in the Sonian Forest](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Brussels_Zonienwoud.jpg/330px-Brussels_Zonienwoud.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Brussels_Zonienwoud.jpg "Old stand of beech prepared for regeneration (note the young undergrowth) in the Sonian Forest") Old stand of beech prepared for regeneration (note the young undergrowth) in the [Sonian Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sonian_Forest "Sonian Forest") - [![Wood](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d8/Fagus_sylvatica_MHNT.BOT.2010.6.81.jpg/330px-Fagus_sylvatica_MHNT.BOT.2010.6.81.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fagus_sylvatica_MHNT.BOT.2010.6.81.jpg "Wood") Wood ### In culture In [Gallo-Roman religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallo-Roman_religion "Gallo-Roman religion"), _Fagus_ (Latin for "beech") was a god known from four inscriptions found in the [Hautes-Pyrénées](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hautes-Pyr%C3%A9n%C3%A9es "Hautes-Pyrénées").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fagus_sylvatica#cite_note-52) ## References 01.
